analysis.one_liner: Treats super PAC spending coordinated with candidates as illegal campaign contributions.
analysis.headline: The bill to treat super PAC spending coordinated with candidates as contributions died in committee without a vote, having no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite campaign finance law so that money spent by outside groups in cooperation with a candidate counts as a campaign contribution, subject to limits and penalties. It would also bar federal candidates and officeholders from fundraising for super PACs and similar groups that accept unlimited money. It was referred to the House Administration committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters who want to know who is funding campaign ads, and candidates who follow the rules rather than relying on unlimited outside money raised in coordination with their campaigns.

how_it_helps.text: The bill defines coordinated spending by outside groups as a campaign contribution, so it would be subject to the same limits, disclosure, and penalties as direct donations [S2] [S3].

It would bar federal candidates and officeholders from soliciting, receiving, directing, or transferring funds for super PACs and other political committees that accept unlimited or undisclosed donations [S3].

It sets penalties of up to 300 percent of the excessive coordinated payment and holds directors and officers jointly liable, and it rejects the common 'firewall' defense that shared consultants does not count as coordination [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Super PACs, candidates who use them, and the donors and consultants who run coordinated outside spending would face contribution limits, disclosure duties, and financial penalties.

drawbacks.text: Coordination is hard to police because campaign staff, consultants, and allied groups often share personnel, so enforcement would fall heavily on the Federal Election Commission, which has frequently deadlocked on such cases; the bill would require the FEC to write new coordination rules but takes effect on a fixed schedule even if the rules are not finished [S3].

Critics of limiting independent spending argue that outside groups spending apart from candidates is protected speech under current Supreme Court doctrine, so parts of the approach would face serious constitutional challenges that could take years to resolve.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real gap: unlimited money flowing to groups that effectively work with candidates while formally staying independent. The cost is that the practical dividing line between independent and coordinated spending is messy, and litigation over the rules could slow the effect. On balance it would strengthen existing limits rather than create new burdens for ordinary donors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Administration committee, which never took it up, and the session ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. David Price of North Carolina introduced the bill on February 18, 2021 [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day, and no further action is recorded [S5].
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died without a markup or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Super PACs, their donors, and candidates who benefit from coordinated outside spending are better off because the bill never advanced; the status quo of largely unlimited outside spending continues.

for.name: Rep. David E. Price
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, his only recorded action on it, and it went to committee with no cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up; it sat at referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote or committee action occurred, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no organized opposition to point to.

industries.industry: Super PACs and outside spending groups
industries.note: Coordinated spending would count as a contribution, capped and disclosed, and candidates could no longer fundraise for them. This closes their main legal advantage over regulated campaign committees.

industries.industry: Political consulting and campaign media firms
industries.note: Consultants working for a candidate who also serve a super PAC would trigger coordinated-spender status for that group, ending the two-client business model built on the firewall defense.
The unlimited channel for backing candidates through coordinated super PAC spending would be capped and exposed to public disclosure.
